Lead Belly recorded over half-a-dozen versions between 1944 and 1948, most often under the title, "Black Girl" or "Black Gal". His first rendition, for Musicraft Records in New York City in February 1944, is arguably his most familiar and is listed as "Where Did You Sleep Last Night". Lead Belly is often said to be the author of the song, e.g. by Nirvana on their MTV Unplugged album in 1994. However, Lead Belly didn't write the song, but reinterpreted it, as did other musicians before and after him. "In the Pines", also known as "Where Did You Sleep Last Night?" and "Black Girl", is a traditional American folk song originating from two songs, "In the Pines" and "The Longest Train", both of whose authorship is unknown and date back to at least the 1870s (though some contend an older, Irish history).

In 1925, a version of the song was recorded onto phonograph cylinder by a folk collector. Bill Monroe had 1941 and 1952 recordings.

I faintly familiar with the VCS3 (I've never played keyboards). My prefered genre of music is 60's and early 70's. Many of those artists used one:

The Alan Parsons Project, Jean-Michel Jarre, Todd Rundgren, Hawkwind, Brian Eno (with Roxy Music and as a solo artist or collaborator), King Crimson, The Who, Gong, and Pink Floyd, among many others. The VCS3-generated bass sound at the beginning of the latter's "Welcome to the Machine" forms the foundation of the song, with the other parts being recorded in response. The Who famously used a VCS3 on "Won't Get Fooled Again" from Who's Next. In this instance the synthesizer was used as an external sound processor, with Pete Townshend running the signal of a Lowrey organ through the VCS3's filter and low frequency oscillators. Yet another notable use of the device (by John Paul Jones) can be heard on the song "Four Sticks" from the untitled fourth album by Led Zeppelin.

I've maybe shared this one before. This is Malmsteen and is being played on a very specific guitar. This guitar is a Fender Strat, but is the Malmsteen signature edition. It's got a slightly hotter set of pickups but, more importantly, the neck is scalloped. That means it has a scalloped fretboard, or that the fingerboard is concave between the frets.

You can do this to your own guitar, but I highly recommend you have a professional do it. I've also seen guitars that people have played so much they were effectively scalloped due to wear and tear!

What does scalloping do? Well, it can fuck you up - first and foremost. See, it gives you the ability to apply more tension and change the tone slightly. So, you need to be very consistent with the pressure you apply. But, because it's scalloped, it also means you can play very fast as it requires a only a very light touch on the strings to effectively fret them. But, you can fret and then moderate the tone to get a slight vibrato effect with great ease. It's mostly used by people who want to play fucking fast.

You know, people like Malmsteen!
